subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: Three boxes numbered I, II, III contain the balls as follows: box I has 1 white, 2 black, 3 red; box II has 2 white, 1 black, 1 red; box III has 4 white, 5 black, 3 red. One box is randomly selected and a ball is drawn from it. If the ball is red, then find the probability that it is from box II.

mark_split.label: Prior probabilities of choosing each container
Probability of the colour from each container

Answer checked: P(R|I) = 3/6 = 1/2, P(R|II) = 1/4, P(R|III) = 3/12 = 1/4; P(R) = (1/3)(1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4) = 1/3; P(II|R) = (1/3)(1/4)/(1/3) = 1/4 — agrees with the book.

recall_prompt: Say how you would find the probability that the red ball came from box II — the events, the priors, the three red-ball probabilities, the total, and Bayes.
insider_note: Each box has a different total (6, 4, 12), so each red probability has its own denominator. The total P(R) comes out to exactly 1/3, which makes the last division short.

steps.label: Define the events
steps.margin_note: First mark. Three box events and one colour event.
steps.memory_tip: Three box events and one colour event — including the boxes not asked about.

lines.text: Let B₁, B₂, B₃ be the events of selecting
box I, box II, box III respectively, and
let R be the event that the ball drawn is red.

recall.must_convey: That B₁, B₂, B₃ are the events of choosing boxes I, II, III and R is the event that the ball is red.
accept: let B one B two B three be choosing box one two three and R be drawing a red ball
define three box events and one red ball event
B one is box one chosen and so on and R is red
moodu boxes ki B one B two B three, red ball ki R
name the three box events and the red event
heard_as: B one B two B three

steps.why: The three box events are mutually exclusive and exhaustive — exactly one box is chosen — so they are the Eᵢ of Bayes' theorem, and R is the A.
common_mistakes: Naming only the box asked about (box II) and no event for the others.

steps.label: Priors
steps.margin_note: Second mark. One of three boxes at random: 1/3 each.
steps.memory_tip: One of three boxes at random is 1/3 each. Do not weight by how many balls a box holds.

lines.text: The box is chosen at random, so

recall.must_convey: That each box has probability 1/3 of being chosen.
accept: each box has probability one third
P of B one equals P of B two equals P of B three equals one by three
the three priors are all a third
prathi box ki probability one by three
one box out of three at random so a third each

steps.why: The prior is the chance of the box before any ball is seen; random selection among three boxes makes it 1/3 regardless of how many balls each box holds.
common_mistakes: Weighting the boxes by their number of balls (6/22, 4/22, 12/22).
Omitting the priors because they are equal.

steps.label: P(red | each box)
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Box I: 3 red of 6. Box II: 1 red of 4. Box III: 3 red of 12. Each over its own box total.
steps.memory_tip: Each over its own box total: 3 of 6, 1 of 4, 3 of 12. Never 22, the grand total.

recall.must_convey: That P(R|B₁) = 1/2, P(R|B₂) = 1/4, P(R|B₃) = 1/4, each red count over its own box total.
accept: red given box one is three by six which is half, box two one by four, box three three by twelve which is a quarter
the red probabilities are half, quarter and quarter
P of R given B one is one by two, given B two one by four, given B three one by four
box one lo red half, box two lo quarter, box three lo kuda quarter
three of six, one of four, three of twelve

steps.why: Each box is its own small experiment; the denominator is that box's total, not the total of all balls.
common_mistakes: Using 22 (all balls) as the denominator for every box.
Reading the red column into the wrong box.

steps.label: Total probability of red
steps.margin_note: Two marks. P(R) = Σ P(Bᵢ)·P(R|Bᵢ). Factor out the common 1/3: (1/3)(1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4) = (1/3)(1) = 1/3.

accept: P of R is a third times half plus quarter plus quarter which is a third times one equals one third
total probability of red is one by three
add the three prior times likelihood terms the bracket is one so P R is a third
P of red ante one by three into half plus quarter plus quarter, bracket one, answer one by three
the denominator comes to one third

steps.why: A red ball can come by three disjoint routes; adding them gives the overall chance of red, the denominator of Bayes' theorem.
common_mistakes: Arithmetic in the bracket: 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4 is 1, not 3/4.

steps.label: Bayes' theorem
steps.memory_tip: 1/4 also happens to be P(R|B₂), so write the Bayes line — the method is the mark.

accept: P of B two given R is a third times a quarter over a third which is one quarter
by bayes theorem the answer is one by four
the box two route one by twelve divided by the total one by three gives a quarter
bayes prakaram one by twelve ni one by three tho divide cheste one by four
the probability it came from box two is one fourth

steps.why: The answer is the share of P(R) that came through box II. Here it equals P(R|B₂) only because P(R) happens to equal 1/3; in general the two differ.
common_mistakes: Answering P(R|B₂) = 1/4 with no Bayes line — the number matches by coincidence but the method is not shown.
